claim: Plasmodium falciparum malaria has been the pre-eminent cause of child morbidity and mortality in the tropics and sub-tropics for much of the last 5000 years.
source: Plasmodium falciparum malaria has been the pre-eminent cause of child morbidity and mortality in the tropics and sub-tropics for much of the last 5000 y.
evidence: This is a general statement about malaria's historical impact, drawing from established scientific knowledge about the disease's epidemiology.

claim: Plasmodium falciparum has had a substantial impact on the human genome through the positive selection of multiple polymorphisms that confer a survival advantage against the disease.
source: As a consequence, it has had a substantial impact on the human genome through the positive selection of multiple polymorphisms that confer a survival advantage against the disease (Williams, 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Williams, 2017.

claim: The rs334 A>T βs sickle mutation in HBB is a malaria-protective polymorphism.
source: The best studied affect the biology of red blood cells (RBCs), which host malaria parasites for most of their life cycle in humans, the rs334 A>T βs sickle mutation in HBB (Williams, 2016), α-thalassaemia (Williams et al., 2005), and blood group O (Fry et al., 2008) all being important examples.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Williams, 2016.

claim: α-thalassaemia is a malaria-protective polymorphism.
source: The best studied affect the biology of red blood cells (RBCs), which host malaria parasites for most of their life cycle in humans, the rs334 A>T βs sickle mutation in HBB (Williams, 2016), α-thalassaemia (Williams et al., 2005), and blood group O (Fry et al., 2008) all being important examples.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Williams et al., 2005.

claim: Blood group O is a malaria-protective polymorphism.
source: The best studied affect the biology of red blood cells (RBCs), which host malaria parasites for most of their life cycle in humans, the rs334 A>T βs sickle mutation in HBB (Williams, 2016), α-thalassaemia (Williams et al., 2005), and blood group O (Fry et al., 2008) all being important examples.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Fry et al., 2008.

claim: The Dantu blood group antigen is associated with high-level protection against severe P. falciparum malaria.
source: Recently, we identified a new variant which is associated with high-level protection against severe P. falciparum malaria to a degree that is close to that of sickle cell trait (HbAS), the strongest malaria-protective condition yet described (Malaria Genomic Epidemiology Network, 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Malaria Genomic Epidemiology Network, 2014.

claim: The Dantu blood group results from a genetic rearrangement within the glycophorin (GYP) cluster.
source: The rare Dantu blood group antigen, which results from a genetic rearrangement within the glycophorin (GYP) cluster, was shown to confer 74% protection against severe malaria in homozygous individuals (Band et al., 2015; Ndila et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Band et al., 2015 and Ndila et al., 2018.

claim: The Dantu blood group confers 74% protection against severe malaria in homozygous individuals.
source: The rare Dantu blood group antigen, which results from a genetic rearrangement within the glycophorin (GYP) cluster, was shown to confer 74% protection against severe malaria in homozygous individuals (Band et al., 2015; Ndila et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Band et al., 2015 and Ndila et al., 2018.

claim: In vitro studies suggest that Dantu protection is explained by the resistance of Dantu RBCs to invasion by P. falciparum merozoites.
source: Subsequent in vitro studies have suggested that this protection is explained by the resistance of Dantu RBCs to invasion by P. falciparum merozoites (Kariuki et al., 2020), thereby preventing infections from progressing to become severe or ultimately fatal.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Kariuki et al., 2020.

claim: 161 healthy adult volunteers living in areas of varying malaria transmission were inoculated by direct venous inoculation with 3.2 × 10³ P. falciparum sporozoites.
source: Briefly, 161 healthy adult volunteers living in areas of varying malaria transmission were inoculated by direct venous inoculation (DVI) with 3.2 × 103 P. falciparum sporozoites (PfSPZ) of Sanaria PfSPZ Challenge (NF54) (Roestenberg et al., 2013; Mordmüller et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim describes the study design and is supported by citations to Roestenberg et al., 2013 and Mordmüller et al., 2015.

claim: The study had 80% power to detect a single variable with an effect size (r²) of 0.3 that accounts for 15% of the variability in parasite growth.
source: With a sample size of 161 individuals, we had 80% power to detect a single variable with an effect size (r2) of 0.3 that accounts for 15% of the variability in parasite growth, as previously described (Kapulu et al., 2018; Kapulu et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim describes the statistical power of the study and is supported by citations to Kapulu et al., 2018 and Kapulu et al., 2021.

claim: Recruitment was restricted to those who were negative for both sickle cell trait and disease.
source: Because of its major impacts on both malaria susceptibility (Allison, 1954) and disease progression (Taylor et al., 2012), and in view of results from a previous CHMI with PfSPZ Challenge conducted in Gabon (Lell et al., 2018), recruitment was restricted to those who were negative for both sickle cell trait and disease.
evidence: This claim describes the study design and is supported by citations to Allison, 1954, Taylor et al., 2012, and Lell et al., 2018.

claim: Venous blood samples were collected twice daily from days 7–14, and then once every day from day 15 until the end of the experiment on day 21.
source: After inoculation, venous blood samples were collected twice daily from days 7–14, and then once every day from day 15 until the end of the experiment on day 21, and screened for parasitaemia by quantitative polymerase chain reaction (qPCR) analysis of the P. falciparum 18S ribosomal RNA gene.
evidence: This claim describes the study methodology.

claim: The endpoint was considered met, and anti-malarial treatment administered, when a threshold of 500 P. falciparum parasites/µl was reached.
source: For each participant, the endpoint was considered met, and anti-malarial treatment administered, when a threshold of 500 P. falciparum parasites/µl was reached.
evidence: This claim describes the study protocol.

claim: Participants were treated earlier if signs and symptoms were observed in association with blood film positivity at any parasite density.
source: Participants were treated earlier if signs and symptoms were observed in association with blood film positivity at any parasite density, and on day 21 post-inoculation regardless of outcome.
evidence: This claim describes the study protocol.

claim: qPCR is much more sensitive than microscopy at low parasite density.
source: While qPCR was used as the primary measurement of parasitaemia because it is much more sensitive than microscopy at low density (Bejon et al., 2006), thick film blood smears were also performed as an additional precaution, and participants were treated if they became blood film positive at any density, an approach that accords with that used in other CHMI studies (Sheehy et al., 2012; Murphy et al., 2012; Hodgson et al., 2014; Kamau et al., 2014; Hodgson et al., 2015; Seilie et al., 2019; Salkeld et al., 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Bejon et al., 2006.

claim: Participants were recruited during 2016, 2017, and 2018 into three successive cohorts from three different malaria transmission zones.
source: Participants were recruited during 2016, 2017, and 2018 into three successive cohorts from three different malaria transmission zones: Kilifi North (no- to low-transmission) and Kilifi South (moderate transmission), both on the coast, and Ahero (moderate to high transmission) in Western Kenya.
evidence: This claim describes the study design.

claim: Kilifi North is a no- to low-transmission malaria zone.
source: Participants were recruited during 2016, 2017, and 2018 into three successive cohorts from three different malaria transmission zones: Kilifi North (no- to low-transmission) and Kilifi South (moderate transmission), both on the coast, and Ahero (moderate to high transmission) in Western Kenya.
evidence: This claim describes the study location characteristics.

claim: Kilifi South is a moderate transmission malaria zone.
source: Participants were recruited during 2016, 2017, and 2018 into three successive cohorts from three different malaria transmission zones: Kilifi North (no- to low-transmission) and Kilifi South (moderate transmission), both on the coast, and Ahero (moderate to high transmission) in Western Kenya.
evidence: This claim describes the study location characteristics.

claim: Ahero is a moderate to high transmission malaria zone.
source: Participants were recruited during 2016, 2017, and 2018 into three successive cohorts from three different malaria transmission zones: Kilifi North (no- to low-transmission) and Kilifi South (moderate transmission), both on the coast, and Ahero (moderate to high transmission) in Western Kenya.
evidence: This claim describes the study location characteristics.

claim: Antimalarial drugs were measured retrospectively in all volunteers using samples collected on both the day before the challenge and 8 days after challenge.
source: Briefly, antimalarial drugs were measured retrospectively in all volunteers using samples collected on both the day before the challenge and 8 days after challenge.
evidence: This claim describes the study methodology and is supported by a citation to Kapulu et al., 2021.

claim: Plasma samples were tested by liquid chromatography-tandem mass spectrometry in two independent laboratories.
source: Plasma samples were tested by liquid chromatography-tandem mass spectrometry in two independent laboratories.
evidence: This claim describes the study methodology.

claim: Sulfadoxine, pyrimethamine, and chloroquine levels were measured at the Strathmore University in Nairobi, Kenya.
source: Sulfadoxine, pyrimethamine, and chloroquine levels were measured at the Strathmore University in Nairobi, Kenya, while artemether and dihydroartemisinin concentrations were measured at the Mahidol Oxford Tropical Medicine Research Unit in Bangkok, Thailand.
evidence: This claim describes the study methodology.

claim: Artemether and dihydroartemisinin concentrations were measured at the Mahidol Oxford Tropical Medicine Research Unit in Bangkok, Thailand.
source: Sulfadoxine, pyrimethamine, and chloroquine levels were measured at the Strathmore University in Nairobi, Kenya, while artemether and dihydroartemisinin concentrations were measured at the Mahidol Oxford Tropical Medicine Research Unit in Bangkok, Thailand.
evidence: This claim describes the study methodology.

claim: The study was conducted at the KEMRI-Wellcome Trust Research Programme in Kilifi, Kenya.
source: The study was conducted at the KEMRI-Wellcome Trust Research Programme in Kilifi, Kenya, and was registered on ClinicalTrials.gov (NCT02739763).
evidence: This claim describes the study location.

claim: The study was registered on ClinicalTrials.gov (NCT02739763).
source: The study was conducted at the KEMRI-Wellcome Trust Research Programme in Kilifi, Kenya, and was registered on ClinicalTrials.gov (NCT02739763).
evidence: This claim describes the study registration.

claim: Genomic DNA was extracted using a QIAmp 96 DNA QIAcube HT kit on a QIAcube HT System.
source: Genomic DNA was extracted following the manufacturer's instructions using a QIAmp 96 DNA QIAcube HT kit on a QIAcube HT System (QIAGEN, Manchester, UK).
evidence: This claim describes the study methodology.

claim: Genotyping for Dantu was performed using ABI TaqMan SNP genotyping Assays-by-Design primers and probes on an ABI 7900HT PCR machine.
source: Genotyping for Dantu was performed using ABI TaqMan SNP genotyping Assays-by-Design primers and probes on an ABI 7900HT PCR machine, as previously described (Kariuki et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim describes the study methodology and is supported by a citation to Kariuki et al., 2009.

claim: Dantu genotypes were inferred from the rs186873296 FREM3 allele, which is in strong linkage disequilibrium with the Dantu structural rearrangement.
source: Dantu genotypes were inferred from the rs186873296 FREM3 allele, which is in strong linkage disequilibrium with the Dantu structural rearrangement (Band et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Band et al., 2015.

claim: The common African form of G6PD deficiency is caused by the G6PD c.202T mutation.
source: We typed for the common African form of G6PD deficiency, caused by the G6PD c.202T mutation (Clarke et al., 2017), the blood group O mutation in ABO (Rowe et al., 2007) and the rs4951074 allele in ATP2B4 (Malaria Genomic Epidemiology Network, 2014) using TaqMan SNP genotyping assays, and for the -α3.7I deletional form of α+-thalassaemia by gap PCR (Wambua et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Clarke et al., 2017.

claim: Of 161 volunteers recruited to the study, 19 were excluded.
source: Of 161 volunteers recruited to the study, 19 were excluded, either because non-CHMI parasite strains were detected in post-CHMI samples (suggesting the presence of coincidental natural infections) (n = 7), or because antimalarial drugs were detected in pre-CHMI samples (n = 12) (Figure 1) (Kapulu et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by data from the study and a citation to Kapulu et al., 2021, and is also shown in Figure 1.

claim: 7 volunteers were excluded because non-CHMI parasite strains were detected in post-CHMI samples.
source: Of 161 volunteers recruited to the study, 19 were excluded, either because non-CHMI parasite strains were detected in post-CHMI samples (suggesting the presence of coincidental natural infections) (n = 7), or because antimalarial drugs were detected in pre-CHMI samples (n = 12) (Figure 1) (Kapulu et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by data from the study and a citation to Kapulu et al., 2021, and is also shown in Figure 1.

claim: 12 volunteers were excluded because antimalarial drugs were detected in pre-CHMI samples.
source: Of 161 volunteers recruited to the study, 19 were excluded, either because non-CHMI parasite strains were detected in post-CHMI samples (suggesting the presence of coincidental natural infections) (n = 7), or because antimalarial drugs were detected in pre-CHMI samples (n = 12) (Figure 1) (Kapulu et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by data from the study and a citation to Kapulu et al., 2021, and is also shown in Figure 1.

claim: After exclusions, data from 142 individuals contributed to the current analysis.
source: After these exclusions, data from 142 individuals contributed to the current analysis.
evidence: This claim describes the study sample size.

claim: 30 individuals were either heterozygous or homozygous for the Dantu allele.
source: Genotyping revealed that 30 of these individuals were either heterozygous or homozygous for the Dantu allele.
evidence: This claim is supported by genotyping data from the study.

claim: Dantu genotype data on 141 out of the 142 participants was used in the downstream analysis.
source: We did not get Dantu genotype data on one individual due to poor quality of the DNA sample; therefore, Dantu genotype data on 141 out of the 142 participants was used in the downstream analysis (Figure 1).
evidence: This claim describes the study sample and is shown in Figure 1.

claim: Infections progressed to the point of reaching the pre-determined treatment threshold of 500 parasites/µl in 25/142 (17.6%) of all volunteers.
source: While infections progressed to the point of reaching the pre-determined treatment threshold of 500 parasites/µl in 25/142 (17.6%) of all volunteers, the proportions varied markedly by Dantu genotype.
evidence: This claim is supported by data from the study.

claim: None of the thirty (0.0%) Dantu carriers reached the treatment threshold of 500 parasites/µl in comparison to 25/111 (22.5%) of the non-Dantu individuals (p=0.01).
source: None of the thirty (0.0%) Dantu carriers reached this threshold in comparison to 25/111 (22.5%) of the non-Dantu individuals (p=0.01) (Figure 2, Table 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by data from the study and is shown in Figure 2 and Table 1.

claim: The difference in the proportion of Dantu heterozygous (0/27; 0%) and non-Dantu individuals reaching the treatment threshold was strongly significant (p=0.004).
source: The difference in the proportion of Dantu heterozygous (0/27; 0%) and non-Dantu individuals reaching the treatment threshold was strongly significant (p=0.004) but did not reach statistical significance in the case of Dantu homozygotes 0/3 (0.0%) because of the small number of individuals in this group.
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of the study data.

claim: 44.1% of the Dantu-negative volunteers developed symptoms that precipitated malaria treatment.
source: Only one quarter (7/27; 25.9%) of the Dantu heterozygotes and none (0/3; 0.0%) of the Dantu homozygotes (Figure 3, Table 2) received antimalarial treatment in comparison to 49/111 (44.1%) of the non-Dantu individuals.
evidence: This claim is supported by data from the study and is shown in Figure 3 and Table 2.

claim: 25.9% of Dantu heterozygous volunteers received antimalarial treatment.
source: Only one quarter (7/27; 25.9%) of the Dantu heterozygotes and none (0/3; 0.0%) of the Dantu homozygotes (Figure 3, Table 2) received antimalarial treatment in comparison to 49/111 (44.1%) of the non-Dantu individuals.
evidence: This claim is supported by data from the study and is shown in Figure 3 and Table 2.

claim: None (0%) of the three Dantu homozygous volunteers received antimalarial treatment.
source: Only one quarter (7/27; 25.9%) of the Dantu heterozygotes and none (0/3; 0.0%) of the Dantu homozygotes (Figure 3, Table 2) received antimalarial treatment in comparison to 49/111 (44.1%) of the non-Dantu individuals.
evidence: This claim is supported by data from the study and is shown in Figure 3 and Table 2.

claim: Multivariate regression analysis revealed that Dantu-carrying subjects overall were administered antimalarial treatment 83% less frequently (OR 0.17; 95% CI 0.04–0.55; p=0.007) than non-Dantu individuals.
source: This analysis revealed that Dantu-carrying subjects overall were administered antimalarial treatment 83% less frequently (OR 0.17; 95% CI 0.04–0.55; p=0.007) than non-Dantu individuals (Table 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by multivariate statistical analysis of the study data and is shown in Table 3.

claim: There were no differences in anti-schizont antibody levels across Dantu genotype groups (p=0.659).
source: We compared anti-schizont antibody levels across Dantu genotype groups and found no differences (p=0.659) (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by data from the study and is shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: The proportion of participants who became PCR-positive at any parasitaemia was similar at 86/111 (77.5%) in the non-Dantu and 20/27 (74.1%) and 2/3 (66.7%) among Dantu heterozygotes and homozygotes, respectively (p=0.745).
source: The proportion of participants who became PCR-positive at any parasitaemia was similar at 86/111 (77.5%) in the non-Dantu and 20/27 (74.1%) and 2/3 (66.7%) among Dantu heterozygotes and homozygotes, respectively (p=0.745) (Figure 4).
evidence: This claim is supported by data from the study and is shown in Figure 4.

claim: Peak parasitaemias reached 9694 parasites/μl in the non-Dantu group in comparison with 411 parasites/μl in the Dantu heterozygotes and only 3 parasites/μl among the Dantu homozygotes.
source: Peak parasitaemias reached 9694 parasites/μl in the non-Dantu group in comparison with 411 parasites/μl in the Dantu heterozygotes and only 3 parasites/μl among the Dantu homozygotes (non-Dantu vs. Dantu heterozygotes p=0.028; non-Dantu vs. Dantu homozygotes p=0.141; and non-Dantu vs. Dantu heterozygotes and homozygotes combined p=0.009) (Figure 4).
evidence: This claim is supported by data from the study and is shown in Figure 4.

claim: The median parasitaemia among those who did become PCR-positive was 112 parasites/μl in the non-Dantu, 13 parasites/μl in the Dantu heterozygous, and 2 parasites/μl in the Dantu homozygous groups, respectively.
source: Similarly, the median parasitaemia among those who did become PCR-positive was 112 parasites/μl in the non-Dantu, 13 parasites/μl in the Dantu heterozygous, and 2 parasites/μl in the Dantu homozygous groups, respectively, although these differences did not reach statistical significance (non-Dantu vs. Dantu heterozygotes p=0.108; non-Dantu vs. Dantu homozygotes p=0.256; and non-Dantu vs. combined Dantu heterozygotes and homozygotes p=0.068) (Figure 4).
evidence: This claim is supported by data from the study and is shown in Figure 4.

claim: Multivariate Cox regression analysis showed that time to treatment was significantly longer among Dantu-carrying than non-Dantu individuals, the overall hazard ratio being 0.39 (CI 0.17–0.87; p=0.022).
source: While the univariate comparisons across genotype groups, performed using the Log-Rank test in the Kaplan–Meier survival curves, did not reach statistical significance (Figure 5a), the multivariate Cox regression analysis with adjustments for other malaria-protective variants, anti-schizont antibody concentration, and location of residence showed that time to treatment was significantly longer among Dantu-carrying than non-Dantu individuals, the overall hazard ratio being 0.39 (CI 0.17–0.87; p=0.022) (Figure 5b).
evidence: This claim is supported by multivariate statistical analysis of the study data and is shown in Figure 5b.

claim: A dose-dependent effect of the Dantu genotype was seen as none of the three Dantu homozygotes required treatment and the time to treatment was significantly longer in Dantu heterozygous than in non-Dantu individuals (HR = 0.41, p=0.042).
source: A dose-dependent effect of the Dantu genotype was also seen as none of the three Dantu homozygotes required treatment and the time to treatment was significantly longer in Dantu heterozygous than in non-Dantu individuals (HR = 0.41, p=0.042) (Figure 5b).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of the study data and is shown in Figure 5b.

claim: No significant differences were seen in any of the study outcomes between the different genotype groups for α-thalassaemia, blood group O, G6PD deficiency and ATP2B4 alleles.
source: No significant differences were seen in any of the study outcomes between the different genotype groups (Figures 2, 3 and 5, Tables 1–3).
evidence: This claim is supported by data from the study and is shown in Figures 2, 3, and 5, and Tables 1–3.

claim: The impact of Dantu on malaria treatment was independent of the presence or absence of other genetic variants in multivariate analysis.
source: As noted above, the impact of Dantu on malaria treatment was independent of the presence or absence of these other genetic variants in multivariate analysis.
evidence: This claim is supported by multivariate statistical analysis of the study data.

claim: This is the first time that Dantu has been shown to protect against early-stage malaria infections.
source: This is the first time that Dantu has been shown to protect against early-stage malaria infections.
evidence: This claim is based on the novelty of the current study's findings.

claim: Dantu protects against severe and complicated malaria by preventing the disease from becoming established in its earliest phase.
source: Our study suggests that Dantu protects against severe and complicated malaria (Ndila et al., 2018; Band et al., 2015) by preventing the disease from becoming established in its earliest phase.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the study data and is supported by citations to Ndila et al., 2018 and Band et al., 2015.

claim: The Dantu genotype protects red blood cells from invasion by increasing their surface tension, which reduces the ability of merozoites to deform their surface and hence productively invade.
source: That mechanistic study revealed that the Dantu genotype protects red blood cells from invasion by increasing their surface tension, which reduces the ability of merozoites to deform their surface and hence productively invade.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a previous mechanistic study (Kariuki et al., 2020).

claim: The tension difference in red blood cells was greater in Dantu homozygotes than heterozygotes, as was the reduction in invasion efficiency, supporting a dose-dependent protective effect.
source: Critically, this tension difference was greater in Dantu homozygotes than heterozygotes, as was the reduction in invasion efficiency, supporting a dose-dependent protective effect.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a previous mechanistic study (Kariuki et al., 2020).

claim: In CHMI studies in malaria-naïve populations, most participants typically develop clinical malaria.
source: In contrast to CHMI studies in malaria-naïve populations, where most participants typically develop clinical malaria (Church et al., 1997), less than one-fifth of the participants in this study reached a threshold of >500 parasites/μl.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Church et al., 1997.

claim: Less than one-fifth of the participants in this study reached a threshold of >500 parasites/μl.
source: In contrast to CHMI studies in malaria-naïve populations, where most participants typically develop clinical malaria (Church et al., 1997), less than one-fifth of the participants in this study reached a threshold of >500 parasites/μl.
evidence: This claim is supported by data from the study.

claim: Most of the participants in the study were residents of malaria-endemic communities and will therefore have been partially immune to the disease.
source: This is probably because most of the participants in our study were residents of malaria-endemic communities and will therefore have been partially immune to the disease.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the study design and location.

claim: In previous analyses of data from the same study, infection outcome was attributable to the degree of prior exposure as estimated by the titre of anti-schizont antibodies.
source: Indeed, in previous analyses of data from the same study we have shown that infection outcome was attributable to the degree of prior exposure as estimated by the titre of anti-schizont antibodies (Kapulu et al., 2022), as well as other measures of exposure including the antibody-dependent phagocytosis of both ring-infected and uninfected erythrocytes from parasite cultures (Musasia et al., 2022) and the breadth of antibodies to P. falciparum Variant Surface Antigens (Kimingi et al., 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Kapulu et al., 2022, Musasia et al., 2022, and Kimingi et al., 2022.

claim: G6PD deficiency, blood group O, the rs4951074 allele in ATP2B4 and α+-thalassaemia have protective effects against severe malaria.
source: Although consistent evidence has been found for protective effects against severe malaria by G6PD deficiency, blood group O, the rs4951074 allele in ATP2B4 and α+-thalassaemia in numerous previous studies (Malaria Genomic Epidemiology Network, 2014; Taylor et al., 2012), none of these polymorphisms had any significant impacts on any of the outcomes under investigation in this study.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Malaria Genomic Epidemiology Network, 2014 and Taylor et al., 2012.

claim: α+-thalassaemia has no effect on either red blood cell invasion or the development of uncomplicated malaria.
source: For example, recent studies have shown that α+-thalassaemia has no effect on either red blood cell invasion (Williams et al., 2002) or the development of uncomplicated malaria (Taylor et al., 2012; Wambua et al., 2006), but protects instead against the development of severe and complicated disease through mechanisms that include the reduced expression of red cell surface antigens that result in cytoadhesion (Krause et al., 2012; Opi et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Williams et al., 2002, Taylor et al., 2012, and Wambua et al., 2006.

claim: α+-thalassaemia protects against the development of severe and complicated disease through mechanisms that include the reduced expression of red cell surface antigens that result in cytoadhesion.
source: For example, recent studies have shown that α+-thalassaemia has no effect on either red blood cell invasion (Williams et al., 2002) or the development of uncomplicated malaria (Taylor et al., 2012; Wambua et al., 2006), but protects instead against the development of severe and complicated disease through mechanisms that include the reduced expression of red cell surface antigens that result in cytoadhesion (Krause et al., 2012; Opi et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Krause et al., 2012 and Opi et al., 2014.

claim: α+-thalassaemia had no apparent impact on infectivity in a previous, smaller, CHMI study using PfSPZ Challenge, conducted in Tanzania.
source: Similarly, it had no apparent impact on infectivity in a previous, smaller, CHMI study using PfSPZ Challenge, conducted in Tanzania (Shekalaghe et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Shekalaghe et al., 2014.

claim: Clinical guidelines mean that controlled human malaria challenge studies only ever reach relatively low-density parasitaemias.
source: Because clinical guidelines mean that controlled human malaria challenge studies only ever reach relatively low-density parasitaemias, they may not adequately capture the impacts of genetic factors that influence the later, more severe stages of malaria disease.
evidence: This claim is based on knowledge of clinical guidelines and CHMI study design.

claim: CHMI studies may not adequately capture the impacts of genetic factors that influence the later, more severe stages of malaria disease.
source: Because clinical guidelines mean that controlled human malaria challenge studies only ever reach relatively low-density parasitaemias, they may not adequately capture the impacts of genetic factors that influence the later, more severe stages of malaria disease.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the limitations of CHMI study design.

claim: CHMI studies can be helpful in pointing towards the pathways leading to severe malaria outcomes for further study by other methods.
source: However, this study shows that they can be helpful in pointing towards the pathways leading to such outcomes for further study by other methods.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the current study's findings.

claim: The Dantu blood group provides strong protection against in vivo parasite growth.
source: In conclusion, this study reveals the power of CHMI studies to deconvolute the malaria-protective effects of naturally occurring human genetic variants, establishes for the first time that the Dantu blood group provides strong protection against in vivo parasite growth, and emphasises the potential of Dantu-phenocopying interventions to limit P. falciparum growth in vivo.
evidence: This claim is supported by data from the study.

claim: CHMI studies can deconvolute the malaria-protective effects of naturally occurring human genetic variants.
source: In conclusion, this study reveals the power of CHMI studies to deconvolute the malaria-protective effects of naturally occurring human genetic variants, establishes for the first time that the Dantu blood group provides strong protection against in vivo parasite growth, and emphasises the potential of Dantu-phenocopying interventions to limit P. falciparum growth in vivo.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the current study's findings.

claim: Dantu-phenocopying interventions have the potential to limit P. falciparum growth in vivo.
source: In conclusion, this study reveals the power of CHMI studies to deconvolute the malaria-protective effects of naturally occurring human genetic variants, establishes for the first time that the Dantu blood group provides strong protection against in vivo parasite growth, and emphasises the potential of Dantu-phenocopying interventions to limit P. falciparum growth in vivo.
evidence: This claim is based on speculation about future interventions based on the study's findings.

claim: The Dantu blood group is associated with 74% protection against severe and complicated P. falciparum malaria infections in homozygous individuals, similar to that provided by the sickle haemoglobin allele (HbS).
source: One such variant is the Dantu blood group antigen, which is associated with 74% protection against severe and complicated P. falciparum malaria infections in homozygous individuals, similar to that provided by the sickle haemoglobin allele (HbS).
evidence: This claim is stated in the abstract and is supported by previous research.

claim: Recent in vitro studies suggest that Dantu exerts protection by increasing the surface tension of red blood cells, thereby impeding the ability of P. falciparum merozoites to invade them and reducing parasite multiplication.
source: Recent in vitro studies suggest that Dantu exerts this protection by increasing the surface tension of red blood cells, thereby impeding the ability of P. falciparum merozoites to invade them and reducing parasite multiplication.
evidence: This claim is stated in the abstract and is supported by previous in vitro research.

claim: 141 sickle-negative Kenyan adults were inoculated with 3.2 × 10³ aseptic, purified, cryopreserved Pf sporozoites (PfSPZ Challenge).
